MISSION: postmortem a real customer failure and make sure it can never happen to a future game-server provision. Then ship the related integrity features.

POSTMORTEM FACTS (verified live today): Paid Minecraft server id cmuo7ajqt0rpohl44gj8triev (hostname minecraft-6b88z1, subdomain tomatikk -> tomatikk.play.nxeon.cloud, node-5 'nxeon-bhs1' region bhs1, vmid 117, public 54.39.132.159:20072 -> DNAT -> 10.20.4.101:25565, SRV record correct). Timeline 2026-09-30: 14:43 someone sent GAME_POWER stop (container 'mc' stopped cleanly, systemd unit minecraft.service inactive); 14:47 customer saved Game settings -> GAME_CONFIG job; it sat QUEUED ~6 min behind inline sweeps, then ran 8s: it only rewrites server.properties over SFTP and restarts nothing unless VERSION changed, so the game stayed stopped. The dashboard showed 'Online' + RAM/CPU/uptime because `running` is derived from `server.status === 'RUNNING'` (VM power state) at app/dashboard/servers/[id]/page.tsx ~1213 and lib/actions-game-control.ts ~170, so the Start button was disabled/hidden and the customer could not start their own game; players got 'Connection timed out'. A later client attempt (owner, ~04:25 UTC Oct 1, from Vietnam) also timed out although container was up/healthy, port 25565 listening in guest, DNAT rule present on node-5, nft forward chain accepts vmbr1, and raw TCP to 54.39.132.159:20072 succeeded from the primary (SGP) and node-2 (Germany) — that one may be boot timing (JVM 26.2 still warming) or path-specific; investigate honestly whether anything platform-side could cause silent SYN drops (rp_filter, conntrack, node firewall, OVH edge, hairpin) and what the provisioning/health pipeline should verify.
Other evidence: worker/index.ts ~1031-1128 provision verifies 'game port never opened on host:port after Ns' — check whether it tests the true public path or something weaker; recent FAILED jobs show 'restart reported active but port never bound' for Minecraft/Valheim (timeout already raised to 180s today in lib/game-control.ts).

DELIVERABLES (all on your branch, verified):
1. Root-cause writeup in docs/DOCUMENTATION.md (+ short incident entry).
2. STATUS TRUTH: define a real 'game runtime state' (VM running? game service active? port answering? intentionally stopped?) — cheap probe (guest agent / ssh `systemctl is-active` + docker state, cached with TTL, never blocking page render) surfaced in customer dashboard + admin: badge must read 'Online' only if the game is actually up, otherwise 'Game stopped' / 'Starting' / 'Not responding' etc.; Start/Stop/Restart availability must follow game state not VM state; if VM runs but game inactive, Start must be available.
3. CONFIG-APPLY SEMANTICS: GAME_CONFIG must never silently leave a server in a worse state: remember run-state before apply; settings that need a restart should say so and offer 'Apply & restart' (restart if it was running; if it was intentionally stopped, leave stopped and say so clearly); no silent no-op.
4. INTENT TRACKING: record customer/admin stop intent so a stopped-by-choice server is distinguishable from crashed; add a fleet sweep that flags 'VM up, game down, not intentionally stopped for >N min' to the admin (alert only; auto-restart behind a per-server/global flag defaulting OFF).
5. AUTO-UPDATE TOGGLE for ALL games: per-server `autoUpdate` (default OFF — updates have broken servers), exposed in game settings UI for every family (with honest copy: for families with no update source say so), honoured by worker/game-update.ts sweep, admin override/visibility, take a safety backup/snapshot before an auto-update when feasible, and log what changed. Audit what worker/game-update.ts does today for each family first.
6. PROVISION GUARD: post-provision readiness checklist for every game (service active, port bound locally, externally reachable via the public IP:port path from a vantage other than the guest — e.g. from the primary — config sane, backup dir, RCON where applicable), recorded on the Server row/job and visible in admin; a failed check must mark the provision as needing attention instead of 'success'.
Schema changes additive only. Write tests where logic is pure. Verify UI states with Playwright in sandbox.

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data, images, or further HTML pages) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. The published path is what the HTML references, relative and with no leading slash. from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

1	# Nxeon — VPS hosting platform
2	
3	Hostinger-style VPS hosting platform running on this Proxmox VE 9 dedicated server (OVH KS-GAME, i7-7700K, 64GB RAM, 2×450GB NVMe ZFS mirror + 4TB HDD backup pool).
4	
5	## Architecture
6	
7	- **Web panel**: Next.js 15 (App Router, server actions) + Tailwind v4, served by `nxeon-web.service` on port 3000, behind nginx on port 80. Public IP: 51.79.162.96.
8	- **Worker**: `worker/index.ts` run by `nxeon-worker.service` (as root — it manages iptables). Polls the `Job` table every 3s and executes provisioning/lifecycle jobs against the Proxmox API.
9	- **DB**: PostgreSQL 17, database `nxeon`, Prisma ORM ([prisma/schema.prisma](prisma/schema.prisma)). Use `npm run db:push` after schema changes.
10	- **Proxmox**: API token auth (`nxeon@pve!platform`, creds in `.env`). Templates: VMID 9000 (Ubuntu 24.04), 9001 (Debian 13), cloud-init based, cloned onto ZFS storage `vmdata`.
11	- **Networking**: VMs attach to NAT bridge `vmbr1` (10.20.0.0/24, gateway .1). IPs allocated from 10.20.0.100–250 ([lib/ipam.ts](lib/ipam.ts)). SSH exposed via DNAT port forwards 20000–29999 in iptables chain `NXEON_FWD`, rebuilt from DB by [worker/network.ts](worker/network.ts) — never edit that chain by hand.
12	- **Cloud-init**: vendor snippet at `/tank/backup/snippets/nxeon-vendor.yaml` (installs qemu-guest-agent, enables root password SSH).
13	
14	## Portals & design system
15	
16	**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.
17	
18	- **Two portals, two shells, deliberately unmerged:**
19	  - `app/admin/**` (admin ops portal) still renders through `components/portal/Shell.tsx` — the ORIGINAL, pre-redesign chrome. Marketing (`app/(marketing)/**`), `/login`, `/register` and admin must stay pixel-identical to how they looked before the redesign. Never edit these expecting Nexion's visual language to apply, and never move Nexion-only styling into a place they can see it.
20	  - `app/dashboard/**` (customer portal) renders through `components/nx/Shell.tsx` — the Nexion redesign. This is where the new design system, its components (`components/nx/*`), and its color/animation language live.
21	  - **A component added to one shell must be added to the other if it's meant to exist on both.** This has silently broken things before: `ComposeProvider`, `TerminalDockProvider`, `MatrixProvider` were each added to `components/portal/Shell.tsx` first and forgotten on `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, taking a whole feature down invisibly (the crash only appeared on a route a smoke test didn't walk).
22	
23	- **The scoping trick that keeps the two visually separate — `app/globals.css`, `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)`:**
24	  Nexion's own colors/tokens and its overrides of shared component classes (`.card`, `.btn-primary`, `.input`, etc.) are NOT bare rules — they're wrapped in `:root:has(.nx-shell-root) { ... }`, a selector that only matches when a `.nx-shell-root` element (rendered only by `components/nx/Shell.tsx`) exists anywhere on the page. That's the entire mechanism keeping marketing/login/admin rendering their original, pre-redesign styles: **do not write a new bare rule for a class both portals share** (e.g. a bare `.card { ... }` outside this scope) — it will apply everywhere, including where it was never meant to.
25	  - Light mode has its own nested scope for the same reason: `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)[data-theme="light"]`, NOT a bare `html[data-theme="light"]`. The bare form loses a CSS specificity fight to the dark `:has()` block regardless of which theme is active — this was a real, session-spanning bug (several "light mode doesn't work on page X" reports all had this one root cause) before it was scoped correctly.
26	  - `.nx-dark-island` is a third scope, deliberately staying dark inside the Nexion portal even when light mode is active (site headers, page hero banners) — it re-declares the relevant tokens back to dark values inside `html[data-theme="light"] .nx-dark-island { ... }`. Add a new always-dark token here too if you introduce one (see `--color-neon-bug` for the pattern: declared in the base `@theme` block, overridden lighter in the light-mode scope, re-declared back to its bright value inside `.nx-dark-island`).
27	
28	- **CSS/JS landmines hit (and fixed) building this — avoid repeating them:**
29	  - **`@keyframes` and `@property` are not valid nested inside a plain style rule** — only inside `@layer`/`@media`/other at-rules. Nesting one inside `:root:has(...) { }` (or any class selector) silently drops it at build time — no error, the animation just never plays, forever, with every other signal (computed `animation-name`, `animation-play-state: running`) looking correct. This broke ~34 animations at once (a levitating icon, the page preloader, several status dots) when a broad `:has()` refactor accidentally wrapped them. If an animation looks "stuck on frame one," check whether its `@keyframes` block ended up nested inside a style rule.
30	  - **`backdrop-filter` on an ancestor creates a new containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.** A `.card` with `backdrop-blur-md` breaks any non-portaled modal/overlay nested inside it (it pins to the card instead of the viewport). Fix: cancel the inherited `backdrop-filter` on the offending class, or `createPortal` the fixed element to `document.body`.
31	  - **A positioned `fixed; z-0` decorative background (an aurora/globe effect) paints above ordinary static content** unless the real content wrapper gets `relative z-[1]`.
32	  - **Hydration-mismatch anti-pattern**: `useState(() => { if (typeof window === "undefined") return X; ...read window/URL...; return Y; })` — the server always takes the `X` branch, the client's first render always takes `Y`, guaranteed mismatch. Read the value server-side (a Server Component's `searchParams` prop) and pass it down as a real prop instead.
33	  - Percentage-based `transform: translateY(%)` inside a flex item whose container has no defined width/height resolves against 0 and silently does nothing — give the container a real dimension (e.g. `inset-0` instead of `inset-y-0 right-0` alone) before debugging the animation itself.
34	  - `git commit -m` with backticks in the message breaks — write the message to a file and use `git commit -F`.
35	  - Bash `cwd` does not persist between tool calls in an agent session — always `cd /opt/nxeon && ...` in the same command.
36	
37	- Design system tokens/classes live in `app/globals.css` + `components/ui/primitives.tsx` (shared/production) and `components/nx/*` (Nexion-only). Charts are dependency-free SVG (`components/ui/charts.tsx`) — do not add a charting library.
38	- Admin impersonation: `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target, `realUser()` the actual admin; banner + exit handled in Shell. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireAdmin` and refuse to render while impersonating.
39	- Metrics come from Proxmox RRD via `/api/metrics` (node for admins, per-server for owners). A server with no `vmid` yet is not "not found" — it's "not provisioned yet," and gets a `{data: [], unavailable: true}` 200 response, not a 404 (a 404 there caused a permanent client poll loop; same fix applied to `/api/servers/[id]/disk`).
40	
41	## Working on this codebase — one tree, any session
42	
43	`/opt/nxeon` (this directory, branch `main`) is the single source of truth. There is no longer a required separate sandbox for ordinary changes — the node-2 box (`/opt/nxeon-v2`) that incubated the Nexion redesign still exists and is safe to use for a large, risky, or highly iterative piece of work (it runs sandboxed: `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` stubs Proxmox provisioning and Stripe charges), but is optional, not a gate. Any session — this one or another — can edit `main` directly and ship through the pipeline below.
44	
45	1. Edit, then `npx tsc --noEmit` before building anything.
46	2. `npm run build` locally only to catch build errors before pushing — do not restart production services from an ad hoc build in this directory (see Commands below); this is validation, not deployment.
47	3. Commit (small, real commits — the GitHub post-commit hook auto-pushes `origin`).
48	4. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh <ref>` — builds, migrates, and restarts staging (`:8080`) from that ref. **Actually look at what you changed there** (screenshot a UI change, click through a flow) before promoting — a change that typechecks and builds can still be visibly broken; this session's own audit caught a large batch of real bugs (broken light mode, frozen animations, missing form validation, wrong prices) that all passed typecheck cleanly.
49	5. `scripts/promote-production.sh` — rebuilds and restarts production from whatever `main` currently has checked out. It refuses to run if staging isn't healthy first.
50	
51	If two sessions are likely to be editing at once, coordinate the ordinary way: pull before starting, small commits, push often (the auto-push hook does this for you on commit).
52	
53	## Integrations (activate via /opt/nxeon/.env)
54	
55	- **Stripe**: `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` + `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` → wallet top-ups switch from demo gateway to Checkout (`/api/stripe/checkout`, webhook `/api/stripe/webhook`, event `checkout.session.completed`, idempotent by session id). Saved cards live in `PaymentCard` (added with the Nexion schema) — a customer who saved a card before that table existed has their card represented only by the older `User.stripeCustomerId`/`stripePaymentMethodId` columns; `hasChargeableCard`/renewals read those directly and are unaffected, but the Billing page's card list reads `PaymentCard`, so a pre-existing card needs the one-off backfill (`scripts/backfill-payment-cards.ts`) to show up there. That backfill has already been run once for every account with a legacy card as of 2026-09-14; it's idempotent, safe to re-run if a new gap appears.
56	- **Namecheap** (`lib/namecheap.ts`): `NAMECHEAP_API_USER/KEY/USERNAME/CLIENT_IP` (+`NAMECHEAP_SANDBOX=1` for testing) → domain search/register/renew/DNS management. TLD retail prices in `TLD_PRICES`.
57	- **GitHub**: remote `origin` = `git@github.com:santino1233/nxeon.git` via deploy key `/root/.ssh/nxeon_deploy`. Every commit auto-pushes via `.git/hooks/post-commit`. `.env`/credentials are gitignored — never commit secrets.
58	
59	## Conventions
60	
61	- All state changes to VMs go through `Job` rows — the web app never calls Proxmox mutation endpoints directly (read-only status calls are OK).
62	- One in-flight job per server (enforced in `serverAction`).
63	- Admin-only actions live in [lib/actions.ts](lib/actions.ts) and must call `requireAdmin()`.
64	- Free VPSes: `Server.isFree = true`, no billing, `expiresAt = null`.
65	- Wallet amounts are integer cents.
66	- Never fabricate: no invented stats, ratings, reviews, player counts, or ETAs. If a number can't be read from the database or a real upstream, the field stays empty and the UI says why — this tree has had hash-derived star ratings and fake reviews removed once already.
67	- Minecraft subdomains (`*.play.nxeon.cloud`) are shared across two tables — `FreeMinecraftServer.subdomain` and `Server.subdomain` — because both products resolve under the same DNS zone. Always check availability through `lib/game-subdomain.ts`'s `isSubdomainAvailable()` (queries both) rather than checking either table alone, or a free and a paid server can claim the same name.
68	
69	## Documentation — keep it current (required)
70	
71	- **Every change, fix, or addition MUST update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` in the same commit.** Add a dated bullet to §15 (Change history) and edit any section the change affects (data model, subsystems, feature catalog, integrations, roadmap, etc.). A commit that changes behaviour without touching the docs is incomplete.
72	- Keep `ROADMAP.md` in sync too: check off / move the item you completed.
73	- `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` is the single source of truth. The public mirror at `https://revsports.ca/docs` is regenerated from it with `node scripts/publish-docs.mjs` (zero-dep markdown→styled-HTML renderer → `/var/www/nxeon-docs/index.html`) — run that after editing the doc so the hosted page matches. The `/docs` nginx location lives in `scripts/configure-domains.sh` so it survives vhost regeneration.
74	- The claude.ai artifact webpage (`https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9b0c97f5-4c34-4f89-bee9-b5a80eb23892`) can only be updated from an interactive Claude Code session (headless/cron runs can't reach it) — that refresh is best-effort, the repo doc + `/docs` page are authoritative.
75	
76	## Commands
77	
78	- Typecheck: `npx tsc --noEmit` (always, before a build)
79	- Build: `npm run build` (must pass before restarting services)
80	- Deploy after changes: `npm run build && systemctl restart nxeon-web nxeon-worker` — or, preferably, go through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → verify → `scripts/promote-production.sh` (see "Working on this codebase" above) so a broken build never lands on a live service.
81	- Worker logs: `journalctl -u nxeon-worker -f`
82	- E2E test: `npx tsx scripts/e2e-test.ts` (orders a real VM; delete it afterwards via a DELETE job)
83	- Admin credentials: `/root/nxeon-credentials.txt`
84	
85	## Domains & TLS
86	
87	- **Single source of truth**: `/etc/nxeon/domains.env` (BASE_DOMAIN, ADMIN_HOST, STAGING_HOST, CERTBOT_EMAIL). The domain is a placeholder (`revsports.ca`) until the real one is bought. **Never hardcode the domain anywhere in app code** — the app uses `APP_URL` / `NXEON_ADMIN_HOST` from `.env`, and nginx vhosts are generated.
88	- **To migrate to a new domain**: edit `/etc/nxeon/domains.env`, point DNS (A records for apex, www, admin host, staging host) at the server, then run `scripts/configure-domains.sh`. It regenerates nginx vhosts, obtains Let's Encrypt certs, updates APP_URL in both `.env`s, and restarts web. That's the whole migration.
89	- **Routing**: customer portal on `https://BASE_DOMAIN` (admin path returns 404 here — hidden); admin ops portal on `https://ADMIN_HOST` (secret subdomain, root 302→/admin); staging on `https://STAGING_HOST`. HTTP→HTTPS 301. Real LE cert (auto-renews via certbot timer); self-signed fallback for bare-IP. A raw `http://51.79.162.96:8080` fallback listener also exists for staging (no TLS, no forwarded headers) — it's a debug path only, not how a real customer or any Server Action's origin check expects to be reached; testing against it directly produces false failures (CSP/origin-check errors) that don't reproduce on the real `STAGING_HOST`.
90	- Secure cookies are on (`COOKIE_SECURE=1`) now that real HTTPS exists. Stripe webhook is live at `https://BASE_DOMAIN/api/stripe/webhook`.
91	
92	## Environments
93	
94	- **Production**: `/opt/nxeon`, DB `nxeon`, services `nxeon-web` (port 3000) + `nxeon-worker`, nginx port 80, VPS pools IP 10.20.0.100–250 / SSH ports 20000–29999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD`. Public: http://51.79.162.96
95	- **Staging**: `/opt/nxeon-staging`, DB `nxeon_staging`, services `nxeon-staging-web` (port 3001) + `nxeon-staging-worker`, nginx port 8080, ISOLATED VPS pools IP 10.20.0.50–99 / SSH ports 30000–30999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD_STG`, VM tag `nxeon-staging`. Public: http://51.79.162.96:8080 (see the TLS note above — prefer `STAGING_HOST` over the bare port for anything that exercises real form submissions). Admin creds: `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt`.
96	- **node-2 sandbox** (optional, not required): `nxeon-fsn1` (178.63.94.114), tree at `/opt/nxeon-v2`, its own DB (`nxeon_v2`), `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` (stubs Proxmox provisioning + Stripe charges only — everything else is real code against a real, separate DB). Useful for large or highly experimental work in isolation; not part of the normal edit→stage→promote path above. Root SSH from node-2 to this box exists (`scripts/node1.sh` on node-2) for exactly that kind of work; treat it the same as any other session touching this box — real prod, no sandboxing here.
97	- Instance differences are driven entirely by `.env` (NXEON_ENV, NXEON_COOKIE_NAME, NXEON_NAT_CHAIN, NXEON_TAG, NXEON_IP_START/END, NXEON_SSH_PORT_START/END, NXEON_CRED_FILE, PORT, APP_URL) — the code is identical.
98	- **Deploy flow**: push to GitHub → `scripts/deploy-staging.sh [ref]` builds+migrates+restarts staging → verify at `STAGING_HOST` (or `:8080`, with the TLS caveat above) → `scripts/promote-production.sh` rebuilds+restarts production. Test changes on staging before promoting — always.
99	
100	## Safety rules
101	
102	- NEVER touch VMIDs 9000–9999 (templates) except to add new templates.
103	- Staging and production share the Proxmox node but never overlap: staging only ever allocates IPs .50–.99 and ports 30000–30999. Never point staging pools at production ranges.
104	- Test risky/provisioning changes on staging (`scripts/deploy-staging.sh`) before promoting to production.
105	- Never `qm destroy` a VM that has a `Server` row — always go through a DELETE job.
106	- Never `pkill -f` by pattern on this box — kill by port PID or systemd unit instead (a pattern match has restarted live production before).
107	- Do not commit `.env`. Do not print the Proxmox token into logs or docs.
108	- Always `git commit` working states; never leave the tree broken — services restart from this directory.

content.thinking:
I'm working out how to resolve the true public address for a game server behind NAT, using the port forward record matching server, guest port, and protocol, falling back to the node's public IP or dedicated IP. Now I'm planning a pure, testable module for the game runtime logic.

I'm defining the possible runtime states—vm_off, online, starting, stopped, crashed, not_responding, unknown—and sketching a function that derives the overall state and UI info from VM status, probe results, stop/start intent, and timing. I'm also planning helper functions to parse the probe script output and build the probe script itself.

For execution, I'm thinking a worker sweep every ~2 minutes probes all running game servers over SSH (checking systemctl/docker state), caches results with a TTL so page renders never block, and refreshes on-demand if stale. I'm sketching a new `GameRuntime` schema model keyed by serverId, storing VM/service/container state, port binding, probe timestamps, errors, derived state, and stop/start intent metadata.

For readiness checks, I'm debating whether to store them as JSON columns on Server versus in the GameRuntime model -- a separate model keeps Server lean and avoids merge conflicts with other agents editing Server, just requiring one added relation field on Server pointing to GameRuntime.

I'm also weighing how failed readiness checks should affect the provision job: rather than failing the job outright, the provision could still complete and mark the server RUNNING while flagging readiness as needing attention so admins can follow up, keeping actual failures (like port conflicts) separate from these softer warnings.

Since provision() is owned by another module, I'll avoid rewriting it and instead add a minimal hook right after the existing game check passes, wrapped in try/catch so it doesn't disrupt the main flow. For admin visibility, I can reuse the existing logError mechanism that surfaces into the admin ErrorLog view rather than building something new.

Next I want to fix a real root-cause bug in the GAME_POWER/GAME_REINSTALL port-check logic — it's checking against the wrong target — by resolving the actual public path through PortForward instead.

I'm sketching a helper that determines the correct check target depending on server type: dedicated servers check the dedicated IP directly, NAT servers resolve the forwarded public port, and primary-node servers check the private IP since the worker runs there too — otherwise skip external checks and just rely on verifyBound. I also realize retries could be a problem: if a GAME_POWER job retries three times after a port-check timeout, it'll needlessly restart the game each time, so I want to mark a timeout failure as non-retriable and need to check whether index.ts already has a mechanism for that.

For the timeout case itself, instead of treating it as a failure, I should record a "not_responding"/"starting" runtime state and notify without retrying, since the service may just be slow to come up.

Now I'm planning intent tracking — recording customer/admin intent (start/stop/restart) on GameRuntime with fields like intent, intentAt, intentBy, and intentSource, while keeping `_serviceState` for backward compatibility and fixing saveGameConfig to stop stripping underscore-prefixed markers, which was the real cause of the false "Online" status. Then I want a periodic fleet sweep job running every couple minutes to check all running paid game servers.

I'm working out the sweep logic: probe each active server over SSH with bounded concurrency and a per-server timeout, update GameRuntime, and if a server stays down past a configurable threshold without being alerted, log it and raise an admin alert plus audit entry. I also want an optional auto-restart path gated behind a flag, rate-limited to once per hour, that enqueues a start job tagged as auto-restart. I'm concerned about SSH probing cost across the whole fleet and realized the existing sweep logic runs inline in the job loop, which already caused a 6-minute delay to another job — so my sweep needs to run fire-and-forget instead of blocking the loop.

Separately, I'm designing how the customer-facing page reads the cached GameRuntime row cheaply, and if the probe timestamp is stale beyond a TTL, a client refresher component triggers a quick server-side SSH probe and refreshes the page without ever blocking the initial render, rate-limited per server. I still need to trace how status and running flags propagate into the panel's buttons so Start remains available when the VM is up but the game itself isn't, and then sketch out what the admin detail page should surface — runtime state, intent, and readiness checks.

For the admin side, I'm weighing where to surface a list of "game down" flagged servers without stepping on the admin nav, which belongs to another area — probably just a section embedded in the existing admin server detail page rather than a new nav entry.

Now I'm working through the config-apply semantics: before applying a game config, probe whether the service is actively running, include a restart flag in the payload for "Apply & restart", and decide post-apply behavior based on that state.

If the family apply recreates the container (version changes for palworld, rust, valheim, bedrock, minecraft), the server ends up started — so if it was intentionally stopped beforehand, I need to stop it again afterward and clearly communicate "left stopped." If apply only writes files like minecraft properties, I handle restart vs. leave-stopped similarly, with explicit messaging about when settings take effect, and if restart wasn't requested but is needed, the UI should surface a clear notification pointing to "Apply & restart."

I also need to verify post-apply state matches the pre-apply state — if it was running before, it must be running and reachable after, otherwise I need to detect failure and attempt recovery rather than silently leaving things broken. This means ApplyOutcome needs a `restarted` flag that each family's apply path sets appropriately, so I should check how minecraft, rust, valheim, palworld, bedrock, cs2, and dayz each handle restarts on recreate. On the UI side, I'm planning to add a "Save & restart" option to the GameSettings component, and separately I'm thinking through an auto-update toggle that applies across all games.

Since game-update currently doesn't do anything meaningful per family (STEAM_APPID is empty), I need to figure out honest, real update sources for each family instead — for Minecraft that could mean fetching the latest Mojang release version and triggering a recreate, while for docker-run families I'd check if pulling a new image digest constitutes a real update, since many of those images already self-update on container start.

Recreating a container requires knowing the original run flags, which is hard to reproduce generically, so I'm leaning toward a more honest approach: some images self-update their game files on restart via their entrypoint, but I can't verify which ones do that without more digging. Given the complexity, I'll define an update-source classifier per game family—distinguishing "minecraft-release" updates from "image-on-restart" updates from "none"—so claims about what gets updated stay accurate.

I should check the seed scripts for known self-updating images like the Valheim server container, but I shouldn't assume behavior without evidence from the catalog comments. Given the scope, I'll keep things honest: a per-server auto-update toggle with per-family copy, a real update path for vanilla Minecraft with backups and changelogs, and image-on-restart handling only for families documented as updating at startup.

For those image-on-restart families (like ETS2/ATS), restarting is how updates apply, but forcing periodic restarts would disconnect players, so I'll keep the copy honest -- "updates apply automatically on restart" -- rather than building complex logic to detect updates without restarting. For "none" families, I'll just say there's no automatic update source. I also want admins to be able to toggle auto-update per server, view the last update result, and have a global kill switch env variable.

Before auto-updating Minecraft, I should back up the world directory into the backup dir, refactoring the existing backup logic into a reusable helper, and log what changed via the audit log plus a notification. I'm also realizing unpinned Minecraft servers already auto-update to the newest release on every restart via itzg's image -- which could explain existing cases of updates breaking servers, since legacy unpinned installs are silently tracking latest.

For the 04:25 timeout, I want to do a read-only SSH diagnosis on node-5: checking rp_filter, conntrack table saturation, nftables rules, and whether OVH's anti-DDoS/game firewall on that IP (BHS datacenter) is involved, since that's known to drop game traffic. I'll check conntrack counts against the max, dmesg for table-full errors, rp_filter settings, and iptables counters on the DNAT rule.

I'm also wondering about the GAME_CONFIG job that ran around 04:22:50 and finished in 33 seconds — if it recreated the container due to a version change, the JVM would still be booting at 04:25, which could explain the timeout, though typically an unbound port gives "connection refused" rather than "timed out" unless docker-proxy behavior differs.

Actually, Minecraft binds its port before preparing the spawn area, so a connection could be accepted while the server is still loading, leaving the client to time out waiting for a handshake response — that timing seems plausible. I should check the container's actual start time via `docker inspect` over SSH to confirm when it came up.

I could use a read-only SSH helper to run that inspect, or go through the node with `qm guest exec` to call docker inspect inside the guest. Let me check how node access is configured, maybe via SSH config entries for root on each node.

The wildcard DNS points to node-2's mc-router at 178.63.94.114, so before a per-server record existed, the client would have hit mc-router with an unrecognized hostname — likely causing it to close the connection or hang, which could explain a timeout rather than a clear error.

Thinking further, if the client's resolver fails SRV lookups entirely (common on some ISP DNS, VPNs, or certain Java client networking paths), it would fall back to the bare A record pointing to 54.39.132.159 on default port 25565 — which lands on node-5, where the firewall's input policy drops the packet silently, producing exactly a "Connection timed out." This gives a plausible, defensible explanation: anything that doesn't honor the SRV record (failed resolver, manual IP entry, direct-connect typed with :25565) ends up hitting a dropped port on node-5, while SRV-aware clients reach the correct, working port. I can't be certain which scenario applies to this particular user, but the SRV-dependency risk is a legitimate platform-side vulnerability worth flagging.

I'm thinking the fix should be either surfacing the IP:port fallback more prominently on the dashboard, or — better — switching the firewall policy on unused game ports from DROP to REJECT with a TCP reset, so misdirected clients get an immediate "connection refused" rather than a silent timeout, which is much easier to diagnose. Changing node firewall policy isn't something I can do myself, so I'll just document this recommendation for the ops team. I'm designing config-apply semantics for the worker: probe the service state beforehand to check if it was running, apply the real config (which always starts the unit), then if it wasn't running before and the intent says it should stay stopped, stop the unit again afterward to honor that intent.

Then I work through the full state-transition matrix: if it was stopped and stays stopped, just note that settings apply on next start; if it was running and still running, check whether a restart was requested or needed and either restart to apply changes or note that a restart is needed later; and critically, if it was running before but ends up stopped after apply, that's a regression — I need to try restarting it, verify success, and fail the job loudly if it doesn't come back up. To detect whether a restart actually happened, I'm thinking of comparing the unit's activation timestamp before and after.

I also need to figure out which config fields actually changed between old and new values, and classify whether any of those changes require a restart to take effect — storing that in the job payload alongside the restart flag. For the UI, I'll offer two clear actions, "Save" and "Apply & restart," with copy that honestly reflects whether the server is currently running. For Minecraft specifically, I'm noting that since server.properties are only read at startup, that same deploy-vs-restart logic will apply there too.

I'm now sketching a generic runtime probe script that resolves the right systemd unit for any game family and reports its status back in a structured way.

It'll query whether the service is active, since when, and how many restarts it's had, then move to the Docker side: listing containers, picking the right one by name, and inspecting its state, start time, and health check status so I can detect whether a change actually took effect.

I'm also thinking about checking bound ports via /proc/net parsing and reading guest uptime from /proc/uptime, all in a single quick SSH exec. For external reachability, I want the worker to do a cheap TCP connect to the true public path for TCP families during the sweep, though UDP can't be checked this way—and I need to consider whether hairpin NAT works when a primary node connects back to its own public IP.

I realize the DNAT in PREROUTING doesn't apply to locally-generated packets, so the primary node's own external check has to honestly be labeled as going through the internal path, while non-primary nodes get a genuinely external check via the primary. Now I'm starting to design a new Prisma model for caching this runtime data, defining a GameRuntime model linked to the Server.

Still writing schema fields...

Auditing the current worker/game-update.ts logic, I realize since STEAM_APPID is unset for every family, the auto-update job today just checks health and reports state without ever actually updating or restarting anything—meaning the "auto-update" toggle is currently just a disguised health check. For real updates, each family has different semantics: minecraft's itzg image resolves versions by VERSION, but only the vanilla variant should safely auto-bump since paper/forge builds need to match customer-selected mods.

For bedrock, I note VERSION can be set to LATEST, which causes itzg to auto-update on restart already, so the toggle there might just mean "restart periodically" rather than fetching new builds itself.

For real Minecraft auto-update implementation, I'm thinking the worker would need to fetch the Mojang manifest, compare to the pinned version, and only apply updates when no players are online -- but checking player presence reliably is tricky given the RCON setup, so I should simplify and avoid overengineering this part.

Before applying an update, I'd back up the world directory using a shared helper, then bump VERSION and run the normal apply path, respecting the run-state semantics so intentionally stopped servers are skipped. The tricky part is rollback: if the new version corrupts compatibility with the old one, simply reverting VERSION isn't safe since downgrading a world that's been opened in a newer version can break it, so at minimum I should alert the admin and preserve the backup rather than attempt a risky automatic restore.

Actually, validateConfig would reject any VERSION not in the schema's options list, so the safer auto-update target is just the newest vetted release already in MINECRAFT_RELEASE_VERSIONS — no network lookup needed. I should go check that schema field and the bedrock VERSION equivalent.

anchor="model GameLogCursor {"
add='''// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// GameRuntime — the truth about the GAME inside a game server's VM.
//
// `Server.status` is the VM's power state. It cannot see the game service
// inside the VM, and the 2026-09-30 tomatikk incident (docs/DOCUMENTATION.md)
// showed what that costs: the game was stopped, the dashboard said "Online",
// Start was disabled, and the customer could not start their own server.
// One row per game server, written by the worker (probes, GAME_POWER,
// GAME_CONFIG, provisioning) and by the inline "refresh" probe on the page.
// Every field is optional/defaulted: a server with no row simply has unknown
// runtime state, which the UI renders as "Checking…" with every power
// control available, never as "Online".
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
model GameRuntime {
  id               String    @id @default(cuid())
  serverId         String    @unique
  server           Server    @relation(fields: [serverId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  // ---- last probe (lib/game-runtime.ts runtimeProbeScript / parseRuntimeProbe)
  probedAt         DateTime?
  probeOk          Boolean   @default(false) // the probe ran to completion (END marker seen)
  probeError       String?
  unit             String?   // resolved systemd unit, e.g. "minecraft.service"
  serviceState     String?   // systemctl is-active: active|inactive|failed|activating|...
  containerState   String?   // docker State.Status: running|exited|restarting|created|...
  containerHealth  String?   // docker health: healthy|unhealthy|starting (when the image has a HEALTHCHECK)
  startedAt        DateTime? // container (or unit) start time — "uptime of the GAME", not the VM
  restarts         Int?      // systemd NRestarts
  portBound        Boolean?  // game port bound inside the guest/container namespace (null = could not tell)
  externalOk       Boolean?  // TCP connect through the public path from the primary (null = not checked / UDP)
  externalTarget   String?   // host:port the external check used
  state            String?   // derived GameRuntimeState at probe time
  stateSince       DateTime? // when `state` last changed
  // ---- run intent: what the owner/admin last ASKED for
  intent           String?   // "running" | "stopped"
  intentAt         DateTime?
  intentBy         String?   // userId of the actor (null = system)
  intentSource     String?   // customer|admin|schedule|auto-restart|config|update|provision
  // ---- fleet sweep (worker/game-runtime.ts gameRuntimeSweep)
  downSince        DateTime? // first probe that saw "VM up, game down, not intentionally stopped"
  alertedAt        DateTime? // admin alert sent for the current down spell
  autoRestart      Boolean   @default(false) // per-server opt-in; global GAME_AUTO_RESTART=1 also enables
  lastAutoRestartAt DateTime?
  // ---- post-provision readiness checklist (worker/game-runtime.ts runProvisionReadiness)
  readiness        Json?     // ReadinessCheck[]
  readinessAt      DateTime?
  readinessOk      Boolean?  // false = provision needs attention
  // ---- auto-update bookkeeping (worker/game-update.ts)
  autoUpdateLocked Boolean   @default(false) // admin override: customer cannot change Server.autoUpdate
  lastUpdateAt     DateTime?
  lastUpdateResult String?   @db.Text
  updatedAt        DateTime  @updatedAt
  createdAt        DateTime  @default(now())

  @@index([state])
}

'''
assert s.count(anchor)==1
s=s.replace(anchor, add+anchor)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

content.content:
## Game server control panel — power, live console/RCON, restarts, worlds

**What it does.** A **Manage** tab (game servers only, injected after Overview in
`components/customer/ServerTabs.tsx`) giving a Pterodactyl/Nitrado-style panel over the customer's own
game VM, entirely on the platform's existing SSH:

- **Power** — start/stop/restart the *game service* (systemd unit), distinct from VM power. `GAME_POWER`
  job → `worker/game-control.ts gamePower`, which resolves the unit from per-family hints and checks the
  `systemctl` exit code (NXGP markers, same "a clean SSH exit proves nothing" discipline as
  `worker/game-update.ts`). In the hero (`components/customer/gamepanel/v2/GameHero.tsx`) the buttons
  are driven by `usePowerGuard` (added 2026-09-30): locked from the click until the real `GAME_POWER`
  job ends — which can be seconds or, with `powerStartTimeoutMs` and up to 3 worker attempts, many
  minutes — with "Starting… 1m 12s" / "attempt 2" shown from real job data, the status pill reading the
  in-flight action, a success/failure line when it ends, and a 5 s cooldown after. `gamePower` enqueues
  under the per-server advisory lock in `lib/job-guard.ts`.
- **Live console** — tails `journalctl`/`*.log` over SSH (inline read) and a command box that speaks
  **Source RCON** to `127.0.0.1:<rcon port>` on the VM **through the SSH connection** (`conn.forwardOut`),
  so the RCON port is never exposed and the password is only ever a protocol packet body, never a shell
  arg. `lib/game-control.ts` (`sourceRcon`, `runRcon`, `readRconCreds`). A **Full log** button (added
  2026-09-27) fetches up to the last 500 lines on demand (vs. the live tail's ~200) for diagnosing a crash
  that already scrolled out of view, on its own tighter rate-limit bucket.
- **Players** — RCON list + kick/ban (player ids allowlisted before templating into an RCON verb).
- **Worlds & backups** — list save entries with sizes; `GAME_BACKUP` job tars the world dir into
  `/var/backups/nxeon-game/<family>-<ts>.tar.gz`, downloaded through the existing `/api/files` route.
  Restore/upload is deferred (download + Files tab for now).
- **Scheduled restarts** — `GameSchedule` rows (daily HH:MM UTC, optional RCON player warning); the
  `gameScheduleSweep()` (~60 s) enqueues a `GAME_POWER` restart when a row falls due and advances
  `nextRunAt`.
- **Danger Zone — wipe & reinstall** (added 2026-09-24) — `GameReinstall` UI component → `reinstallGame`
  action → `GAME_REINSTALL` job → `worker/game-control.ts gameReinstall`: stops the game's systemd unit,
  `docker rm -f`s its container, wipes the CONTENTS of its real bind-mounted data directory(ies) (parsed
  straight from the family's own setupScript `-v host:container` flags — `dockerHostMountsFrom`,
  `worker/game-variant.ts` — never a guessed path), then re-runs a freshly rebuilt setup script
  (`buildGameSetupScript`, same pipeline `PROVISION` uses: reapplies the customer's CURRENT
  gameVariant/gameConfig and mints brand-new secrets for palworld/rust/cs2 — a real fresh install, not a
  stale replay). Requires typing "WIPE" to confirm. Never touches the underlying VPS/VM (no Proxmox call,
  no vmid/IP/SSH-host-key change) — only the game. Full "change game" (swap to a different family) is
  **not implemented** — this always reinstalls the SAME family; a real family swap needs a different
  OsTemplate/GamePlan/ports/RCON setup and is left as a documented follow-up. (Previously the Danger Zone
  subtitle promised "Reinstall, wipe or cancel" but only cancel existed — audit finding 2026-09-24.)

**Per-game RCON coverage** (extended 2026-09-24). Source RCON is wired for **Minecraft, CS2, Palworld**
(creds read from a config file — `server.properties` / `server.cfg` / `PalWorldSettings.ini`) and now
also **ARK: Survival Evolved, ARK: Survival Ascended, Team Fortress 2, Left 4 Dead 2, Project Zomboid**
(creds read from the docker container's own env via `docker inspect` — `source: "docker-env"` in
`RconConfig` — verified against each platform image's real entrypoint; ARK/ARK:ASA in particular never
write their RCON password to any file on disk at all, so a file-based reader could never have worked for
them). **Squad** genuinely speaks Source RCON too, but the platform's image (`cm2network/squad`) ships it
with no password ever configured — a provisioning gap, not a protocol gap, left as a documented follow-up
rather than shipping a console that would always fail auth. **Killing Floor 2** has a real admin surface
(Tripwire's WebAdmin) but it's HTTP, not the Source RCON binary wire this file speaks — different
transport, out of scope. **Rust** uses WebSocket RCON — still deferred. **Valheim / Terraria** and every
other family with no confirmed Source-RCON wire have no native remote console — the command box is
disabled with a note. Power, logs, world backups, schedules and reinstall work regardless of RCON support.
Per-family facts live in `GAME_CONTROL` (`lib/game-control.ts`), which also documents exactly which
families were researched and why each verdict was reached.

**Files.** Actions `lib/actions-game-control.ts` (ownership-guarded, rate-limited, SANDBOX-synthetic
reads); transport + validation `lib/game-control.ts`; worker `worker/game-control.ts` +
`worker/game-variant.ts` (setup-script substitution/wrap, shared with `PROVISION`); UI
`components/customer/game/GameManage.tsx` + `components/customer/gamepanel/v2/GameReinstall.tsx`. Schema:
`GameSchedule` + `JobType.GAME_POWER/GAME_BACKUP/GAME_REINSTALL`.

**NAT (non-dedicated-IP) join-port coverage** (extended 2026-09-24). Only a game's primary join port used
to get auto-forwarded for a NAT server; extra ports a game genuinely needs (beyond the one `joinPortFor`
names) live in `GAME_EXTRA_JOIN_PORTS` (`lib/games.ts`) and are forwarded automatically by the same loop
that already handled Valheim's 3-port case. Verified 2026-09-24 against each game's own official
docs/wiki and extended for **Satisfactory** (7777/udp+tcp, 8888/tcp — the last is required, not optional,
or clients hang on "loading"), **The Isle Evrima** (10000/tcp queue port), **Sons of the Forest**
(27016/udp + 9700/udp — the server self-checks all 3 and refuses to start otherwise; corrected the
audit's own guess that 9700 was the GamePort — it's actually the existing 8766), **The Forest** (27016/udp
+ 8766/udp), **Squad** (27165/udp query + 15000/udp beacon — both part of the real UE join/queue
handshake, not cosmetic), **ARK: Survival Evolved** (7778/udp, medium confidence — Steam P2P advertising),
and **Project Zomboid** (16262/udp direct-connect channel). Also fixed **Conan Exiles**, which forwarded
7777 as **TCP** (Funcom's own docs: that's the mod-download port) instead of the real **UDP** join port —
audit finding: "Conan has never been joinable via NAT." Still unverified and deliberately not touched:
gmod/unturned/factorio (27015-27017 range) and eco/empyrion/stationeers (27015-27016 / 30000-30003
ranges) — each publishes more than its single join port and needs the same live/documented verification
before extending.

content.content:
### 2026-09-30 — Real customer bug: Terraria "start" falsely reported as failed while the server was actually booting fine

Reported live by a real customer (throarbin-terraria, node-5): every Start after the first one appeared
to do nothing — button grayed out, then reset, no server. Root-caused via direct SSH to the real VM:

- The container WAS actually running and had already booted successfully — `docker logs` showed
  `Listening on port 7777` / `Server started` well after the platform had already reported the job FAILED.
- `worker/game-control.ts`'s `GAME_POWER_PORT_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS` (30s) is too short for Terraria's real
  boot: world loading + "Settling liquids" (scales with world size), plus recovery time from a prior
  improper shutdown (`terraria.service`'s `ExecStop=docker stop -t 30` doesn't guarantee TShock's own
  console gets a clean `exit` — flagged separately below, not fixed here). The existing code comment
  claimed a slow family "only delays the SUCCESS notification, never falsely reports failure early" —
  that was incorrect; the timeout genuinely throws and fails the job.
- **Fix**: added `GameControlSpec.powerStartTimeoutMs` (optional per-family override, `lib/game-control.ts`),
  set to 180s for `terraria`, wired into `worker/game-control.ts`'s port-check call. Corrected the stale
  comment on the 30s default to describe what actually happens on timeout.
- Confirmed live: the customer's actual server is healthy right now (`docker ps` showed 3h uptime,
  logs confirm a clean listen on 7777) — the bug was purely the platform's own false-failure report, not
  data loss or a real crash.

**Not fixed here, flagged as a follow-up**: `terraria.service`'s stop path sends `docker stop` (SIGTERM),
which the `ryshe/terraria` image doesn't appear to translate into TShock's own graceful `exit` console
command — the container's logs show "TShock was improperly shut down" after a normal stop. AutoSave is
enabled so data-loss risk looks low, but a real fix (piping a clean `exit` into the console before the
stop signal, or confirming the image already handles SIGTERM correctly and this message is a red herring)
needs real verification against a live container, not assumed.

**Files:** `lib/game-control.ts`, `worker/game-control.ts`.

### 2026-09-30 — Power controls can't be spam-clicked any more (VPS + game), and the backend "one job per server" guard is now actually atomic
- **Fix**: new nullable `Server.guestSshPort` column (additive, `db push`'d — changes nothing for any
  existing server, since `null` falls back to `?? 22`, today's exact behavior). `connectionTarget()`'s
  dedicated-IP branch now reads `server.guestSshPort ?? 22` instead of a bare `22`. Selected into
  `lib/actions-files.ts`'s server query (the Files feature); `worker/firewall.ts` already `include`s
  the whole row so it picked it up for free. New unit tests in `test/sftp-connection-target.test.ts`
  pin both the override and the (unchanged) default. Admin server detail page now shows "Guest SSH
  port override" for any server with a dedicated IP, so this doesn't stay a hidden DB-only field.
- **The firewall side needed a second, separate finding**: even with the port fixed, `syncFirewall`
  would still fail — this guest's `iptables` (legacy) returns "Incompatible with this kernel" (likely
  1Panel's own nftables-only setup). Checked the LIVE guest directly: `iptables -L INPUT` showed only
  UFW's own chains (`ufw-before-input` etc.), policy DROP — confirming the platform's `NXEON_FW` chain
  has in fact never once been successfully applied to this guest, so there was nothing live to
  "detach". The customer's 6 stale `FirewallRule` DB rows are display-only leftovers; deleting them
  requires no guest-side sync (and syncing them now would risk appending a default-DROP that doesn't
  know about port 2222 — `FW_KEEP_OPEN_TCP_PORTS` only keeps 22 open — so deliberately did NOT trigger
  a sync). `SYNC_FIREWALL` jobs are only ever created by `lib/actions-firewall.ts` on an explicit rule
  edit (confirmed — no periodic/cron trigger exists), so once those 6 rows are gone, nothing re-fires
  on its own.
- **Not yet done**: deleting the 6 stale `FirewallRule` rows was blocked by the auto-mode permission
  classifier ("Modify Shared Resources") on a direct DB write — needs the owner to run it or grant it.
  Worth a platform-wide follow-up too: any guest running an nftables-only setup (1Panel defaults to
  this) can never successfully use the panel firewall feature at all, independent of this port issue.

**Files:** `prisma/schema.prisma`, `lib/sftp.ts`, `lib/actions-files.ts`,
`app/admin/servers/[id]/page.tsx`, `test/sftp-connection-target.test.ts`.
